newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW - Apache bullish on Australia.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW - Apache bullish on Australia.

text.p: Houston-based energy group Apache Corp plans to spend about US$83 million in Australia in 1997 out of a worldwide budget of US$200 million, a company official said on Friday.
The funds are being spent in the Carnarvon Basin offshore Western Australia, managing director of Perth-based unit Apache Energy Ltd, John Crum, told Reuters in an interview.
Larger international oil companies have come to the Basin to tap into world-class fields such as the North West Shelf and Barrow Island.
But Crum said plenty of opportunities exist for smaller players.
Apache operates the 11,000-barrel a day Harriet island oil and gas field and is developing the nearby Agincourt and Stag fields in the basin.
This year Australian operations should add 2.5 million barrels of oil equivalent (BOE) to Apache's worldwide production of some 67.5 million BOE, Crum estimated.
"Australia is critical to Apache, especially in its international effort," he said.
"We've gone from spending US7.2 million in 1993 to US$52 million in 1996 and 1997 will be US$83 million," he said.
Crum said Apache intends to continue allocating a significant portion of its entire budget in Australia, due in large part to upcoming development expenses in Western Australia.
This year, Apache plans to drill 17 exploration wells, most likely representing Australia's largest exploration programme for the year, Crum said.
"It's going to be our most aggressive programme and the most aggressive programme in the Carnarvon Basin for a number of years," Crum said.
Last year, Apache drilled 10 wells in the Carnarvon Basin.
"We aren't looking for the same things the majors are looking for ... We clearly understand we are playing in a different league than Woodside Petroleum Ltd and Chevron and Shell," he said.
Crum said Apache's focus is on smaller-sized fields, with reserves of between 20 and 50 million BOE.
"We see that as a niche we can fill," he said.
Crum said he views the Carnarvon Basin largely untapped.
"It's under-explored in the sense that you're not seeing much activity year after year," he said.
In 1996, the basin attracted only 15 exploration wells and 10 appraisal wells in total, Crum said.
"You see more wells like that drilled in a week in the Gulf of Mexico ... Certainly there's a lot of room to run," he said.
He said Apache has looked at properties elsewhere in Australia but remains focused exclusively on the Carnarvon Basin.
"Apache realises it cannot be all things to all people," he said.
Australia is one of two key focal points internationally for the company, Crum said.
The other is in the Kharda concession in the Western Desert of Egypt where the company has interests in 19 million acres.
Internationally, it also operates the Zhao Dong offshore block in China, with a 50 percent interest.
